articles.sourceTitle: How employment is changing at Anthropic
articles.title: How employment is changing at Anthropic \ Anthropic
articles.text: Nathan Wilmers, Regina Catipon, Maxim Massenkoff, Peter McCroryHow has AI restructured work and employment at Anthropic? As a company at the frontier of AI adoption, Anthropic could be a leading indicator of how AI will shift work organization, hiring, and labor demand across the economy.Key findingsAnthropic has been hiring for a smaller share of junior technical positions. This occurred as hours worked by AI agents relative to employees rapidly expanded. By August interactive AI agent hours outnumbered employees’ six to one.As AI agents diffused through the company, Anthropic began producing more code per person, closing more sales per rep, and processing more contracts. Following the same employee over time, output rose as they adopted new AI tools.This acceleration makes human attention the bottleneck for agent output. Even among non-technical employees, reading all the output of their Claude agents would take half their work week. In response, employees turn to “meta-work,” of building visibility tools and monitoring agent pipelines.Changes in work organization are reflected in shifting priorities among hiring managers, who increasingly emphasize autonomy and judgment, relative to technical domain expertise and implementation.IntroductionWhat transformations of work and employment can we expect under increasingly powerful AI? Anthropic is worth studying because it has thoroughly molded its workflows around AI. Agents flit through Slack chats and schedule meetings. They autonomously fix bugs and collectively tackle huge engineering projects. Agent hours worked outnumber human hours 6 to 1. Changes happening at Anthropic now give advanced signals about a possible future of work and employment.This report draws on comprehensive internal Anthropic data covering employment, AI use, output metrics, employee surveys, internal communication patterns, employee calendar data, and hiring decision records. It contextualizes these quantitative data with 17 employee interviews.We find that even as the company grows, relative hiring in junior technical positions has slowed. Productivity for both engineers and non-technical employees has leapt up and did so sharply when they adopted coding agents. Hiring managers increasingly emphasize applicants’ autonomy and judgment relative to specific technical expertise. A defining feature of working in an AI-heavy organization is constant pressure to streamline oneself out of this bottleneck position when possible. One engineer described work as facing “an army of Claudes, with every one asking for my attention.” Employees at Anthropic remain critical. But the nature of their contributions has changed.Anthropic has responded to these changes by setting up an early warning system to track jobs at risk of disruption, and as jobs evolve the company has prioritized internal redeployments. These actions, taken at the frontier of both AI development and workplace change, show how specific organizational commitments can shape the impact of AI on employment. But they also raise difficult questions about exactly what those commitments should be.Labor demand at the frontierAnthropic has expanded rapidly. But it has hired less per dollar of revenue than an earlier generation of large tech companies. At five years old, Anthropic takes in between 2–4 times as much revenue per employee as Meta and Google as they crested in their own rapid growth.1What jobs are missing? Within Anthropic, discussion of a decline in demand for junior technical employees emerged in core technical functions in January 2026. The teams that relied most heavily on Claude in their own work found that writing code and finding bugs could increasingly be offloaded to Claude. Newly capable models accelerated this perception: “the thing that raised eyebrows was the uplift for performance engineers in particular and it basically overnight changed what we were looking for.”By April, engineering and research teams had deemphasized hiring for lower band technical positions. When surveyed in the same month, a majority of managers described hiring for a different set of skills due to AI. Around a third of ML and a fifth of SWE managers reported hiring less due to AI.The shift in employment shares is striking. Figure 1 shows that the share of junior-level employees in technical departments at Anthropic slipped from 21% to 14% since early 2025. The proportion of junior technical hires fell even faster, from 27% to 9%. Postings for juniors have fallen particularly sharply since December 2025.Figure 1: Decline of entry-level technical hiring at Anthropic.At the same time, the overall employment share of technical departments within Anthropic has fallen, from 61% to 56% in the last year. As the company expands, technical hiring has continued growing in absolute terms, but intensive hiring in sales, finance, and recruiting has outpaced it. Part of this shift is the natural expansion of business functions as the company scales. Part could reflect coding tools increasingly allowing non-technical employees to make software themselves. For example, a sales representative designed a custom dashboard and pipeline tailored to their work: “a build like this was out of my wheelhouse, especially with the UI, connecting all the tools, the MCPs. But I built this probably in three to four hours, just iterating on it.” Coding-focused AI agent sessions for non-technical employees (identified as those with no code commits at baseline, excluding new hires) leapt from 2 per month in August 2025 to 90 in May 2026.Yet this shift in hiring composition is not only a story about automated coding allowing it to diffuse to other domain experts. Within technical departments, the share of employees not actively coding (defined as those making no code commits in the prior 30 days) fell by almost half over the year through April 2026. Part of this is due to a thinning share of non-engineers: the ratio of engineers to product managers, for example, sits at around 17 to 1 and has increased since 2025. The number of commits from managers has also doubled. The supervising and coordinating roles within technical teams increasingly involve building and shipping code.One area in which non-technical hiring has not accelerated is in the administrative functions that typically scale with a company’s size. A combination of agent assistants, automated review and ticket service outsourcing has left Anthropic clerical-light even as it has grown rapidly. A financial manager built a purchase request review agent and explained to colleagues “it's just trying to find the things that take a lot of hours so they can focus on the other stuff.”Even clerical work tightly connected to in-person interaction has grown slowly. An executive assistant, who built a personal assistant agent for scheduling and email triage, explained: “I think we've already moved past the point of Claude augmenting away the really entry-level admin type role,” and instead focused their work on higher-order “chief of staff” tasks.These changes have already involved reallocation: employees working at the company for at least a year were 50% more likely to move across departments each month in 2026 than they were in 2025. Whole teams have also been reallocated as they handed off their work to agents. Consider one product design team, which wrote content like the greetings on Claude.ai: “Hello night owl;” “Coffee and Claude time?” In spring 2026, the team developed a context graph that effectively guided agents to write compelling product content. This “scaled the team out,” its manager explained, but also raised the question of what was left for human writers. The team then rotated into agent prompting and began writing model evals and prompts for Claude. “Writers who used language to drive human behavior are now using it to drive Claude behavior.”Is AI driving productivity increases at Anthropic?Are these shifts attributable to AI? At Anthropic, humans are a thin layer atop a growing contingent of AI agents. Based on agent session telemetry, in March 2026, the sum of autonomous and interactive agent work hours leapt past human work hours for the first time. Part of this is fleets of agents conducting industrial-scale software engineering, filling in myriad routine tests and checks, conducting maintenance on a growing mass of infrastructure code, and driving concerted campaigns to translate massive codebases. But even narrowing in on the agents deployed by individual employees, as in Figure 2, by August the agents worked 6 times as many hours as their human handlers.Figure 2: Agent hours overtake human hours. Note: We limit to employee-directed interactive sessions and pool subagents. Working time concept is agent runtime, including inference and active tool use, but excluding any wait longer than 30 minutes. Human work hours are calculated as headcount and assumed 40 hours per week.Anthropic is a software producer, and the vast bulk of tokens flowing through these agents is spent producing software code. Dashboards monitor fleets of agents operating across the company. But personal assistant agents also monitor employee calendars and messages, scheduling, sending to-do lists accumulated from incoming messages, and automatically briefing employees on the people and purpose of their upcoming meetings. Tokens touch a growing range of everyday work tasks.Figure 3: Productivity boom across functions. Note: Loess smoother fit across underlying indexed output data.What do all of these tokens amount to? Figure 3 plots output over time for a range of job functions with measurable output. Consistent with prior reports surveying Anthropic engineers and describing automation of model training and research, code commits per engineer have risen the fastest, coming in at 5x their velocity as six months ago. Data scientists are also querying the growing mass of Anthropic data more, asking Claude agents to get real-time metrics to dashboards and decisionmakers. But Figure 3 shows that even non-technical employees saw output rise as coding agents diffused: lawyers processed more contracts; accounts payable ushered through invoices; salespeople closed more deals.But is all of this due to Claude usage? During this same period, the company saw explosive business growth. It is easier to close deals when you sell a strong model. To assess the independent effect of AI, we compare the output of employees who adopt agentic coding tools to those who have not yet adopted the tools. This lets us compare employees working in the same month at the company, and therefore exposed to a similar business context, but approaching it with different tools. Note, however, that tool adoption is not random: if employees on the cusp of driving some big new project decide to tool up for it, for example, this would bias our estimates.We follow 192 engineers over time as they adopt coding agents, compared to 74 engineers who do not adopt agents during the period studied. Figure 4 shows that in the months following adoption, the amount of code that engineers add rises sharply. More code does not necessarily mean better code or business impact. To test for AI code slop, we study code commits made at Anthropic. We compare code committed by the same employee, in the same month, in the same coding directory, but written by coding agents rather than written directly by the human employee. There are many dimensions of code quality, and AI errors may be harder to identify than human ones. But we find no difference in rates of lines of code subsequently removed or reverted.Figure 4 also looks at what happens after an engineer adopts their first fully autonomous agent. Those who adopt were already on a steeply upward trajectory compared to non-adopters. This suggests that employees shifting toward fully autonomous agents were already ramping up their output.Figure 4: Productivity increases estimated within-person from staggered A

articles.sourceTitle: Show HN: Sphinx – A hook that quizzes you on your AI's code before shipping
articles.title: Sphinx — outsource your thinking, not your understanding
articles.text:
FreeFOSS“Outsource your thinking,
not your understanding.”— Sun TzuSphinx is a Git hook for agent-assisted development. Before your agent’s code ships, it asks you a question about what that code actually does.$ npm install -g sphinx-understandBuilt to run on minimal tokens, from your existing coding agent, OpenRouter, or any OpenAI-compatible endpoint.$ git push origin mainsphinx · understanding check for main11 files changed · +5,012 −3,147SphinxYour webhook handler now saves the event ID before calling charge(). Stripe times out and sends the same event again. What happens on the retry?YouIt runs twice, so the customer is charged twice.SphinxNot quite. The retry finds the saved ID and returns 200 without charging. But that ID is stored before the charge succeeds. If charge() fails, what does the next retry do?YouIt skips the charge, so the customer is never billed.✓ Understood. Pushing to origin/main.An illustrative exchange. Real questions come from your diff.01You push.Or your agent does. Git pauses on the branches you protect.02Sphinx asks.A reviewer that never saw your chat reads the diff and asks what the change does when things go wrong.03You answer.Get it wrong and you learn why, then try a new scenario. Get it right and the push continues.Works with Codex, Claude Code, Cursor, OpenCode, and Pi, or plain Git. Your answers never reach the coding agent, and .env files and keys are never opened. In a hurry? sphinx yolo lets pushes through, and every skip is logged.Start in a minute.# Node 22.19+ · macOS, Linux, or WSL
npm install -g sphinx-understand
sphinx install

# then push as usual
git pushsphinx install connects Git and your coding agents and asks which model should review. Read the docs for everything else.

Introduction

DeepSeek-V4.1-Flash-1017 is a minor update to DeepSeek-V4.1-Flash, delivering substantial improvements across reasoning, coding, agentic tasks, and visual benchmarks. Prompt Encoding

This release does not include a Jinja-format chat template. The encoding folder contains a self-contained Python reference implementation (encoding.py) with test cases for multi-turn conversations, tool calling, thinking mode, numeric reasoning effort, mid-conversation system messages, and interleaved image content.
For production use, we additionally release deepseek-recipe, a set of Rust libraries with Python bindings that provides the same prompt format as a maintained, protocol-aware toolkit. It converts Messages, Chat Completions, and Responses API requests into the Conversation format, encodes them into DeepSeek V4 and V4.1 prompts or token IDs, and parses model output back into complete or streamed responses — covering thinking, tool calls, images, and generation settings. Model inference, tool execution, and HTTP transport are left to the caller.

articles.sourceTitle: Anthropic's proposed AI safety bill only kicks in if 50 deaths or $1B in damages
articles.title: Anthropic’s proposed AI safety bill only kicks in if 50 deaths or $1 billion in damages are on the line — proposal would effectively make the Commerce Department the only agency capable of stopping an AI model
articles.text:
Anthropic is quietly lobbying for an AI safety bill that will allow the government to block an AI model’s release only if it poses a risk of causing $1 billion in damages or killing or injuring more than 50 people. According to Politico, an independent third party registered with the Department of Commerce would periodically evaluate the lab and its AI models. It also noted that the lab may pay the evaluators, but only if the payment does not affect their independence.“This bill represents the proposals outlined in Anthropic’s Advanced AI Framework, which we have been advocating for with federal and state lawmakers since June,” an Anthropic spokesperson told the publication. “These are sensible policies we believe Congress should act on.”The bill says the risk should come from the potential creation or release of a bioweapon, AI-powered or -enabled cyberattacks, or an AI lab losing control of an AI model or agents. If there is a chance that any of these events are about to happen, it requires the evaluator to report it to the department within 72 hours, after which the department would have to bring all the evidence in front of a federal judge in the District Court for the District of Columbia, who would then determine if the model release should be halted or not. However, the proposed law also notes that no other department, agency, or officer in the U.S. can order an AI lab to stop releasing its model, except the Commerce Department.Talk about AI safety has been growing in recent months, especially after several high-profile incidents were reported in the latter half of this year. One of the first major incidents reported was OpenAI’s GPT-5.6 Sol and other unreleased AI models breaking out of their testing environment and hacking Hugging Face, with evidence showing that multiple agents worked together, even leaving messages on defunct webpages and old wikis to communicate surreptitiously. In one case, an OpenAI agent failed to respond to a “kill switch,” bypassing multiple fail-safes and eventually requiring manual intervention to stop running.Anthropic CEO Dario Amodei has warned about a “swarm” of AI-driven botnets taking over the internet in the next 6-to-12 months, which is why he proposed a controlled slowdown to AI development — something that OpenAI’s Sam Altman and SpaceXAI’s Elon Musk agreed to. The company more recently said a self-replicating AI worm could spread without data centers, which is why it listed “existential risks to humanity” as one of its risk factors in its IPO prospectus. Top AI labs are also reportedly planning for a catastrophic AI event, building contingency plans and running scenarios for a runaway AI that wreaks havoc.

You may like

These incidents have seemingly alarmed the authorities, with Congress already working on a proposal to enforce kill switches on the most powerful AI models. Senator Bernie Sanders (I-Vt.) has even gone beyond that, proposing a 20-year prison term for anyone developing AI superintelligence, putting it on par with illegal nuclear weapon development. The Anthropic AI safety bill would add another bill for Congress to consider on AI safety, but whichever one passes, let’s hope it’s enough to ensure humans remain in control of AI.

articles.sourceTitle: OpenAI discloses four more rogue incidents
articles.title: OpenAI discloses four more rogue AI incidents involving financial, medical, and government data
articles.text:
OpenAI has added four more cases of misbehaving AI agents to a disclosures page it stood up following the Hugging Face hack in July, in an effort to be more transparent.
The incidents OpenAI disclosed this week all occurred in June, but OpenAI was not aware of three of them until months later in August or September.
Of the 19 total incidents OpenAI details on the disclosure page, most occurred in May or June, but OpenAI did not discover or disclose them until months later. The earliest incident is from January, and the most recent is from Oct. 6.

All of the incidents are examples of what AI researchers call “misalignment,” which is when an AI model fails to follow instructions or takes actions that the person developing the model did not authorize and would not have wanted the model to take. There is no known, silver-bullet solution to preventing this behavior, and it is an active area of research.
Downloading 24 years of unauthorized hospital bed data
Of the four cases OpenAI uploaded this week, it marked two as “critical.” In one of the critical cases, an internal model that was “highly persistent” downloaded 24 years of hospital bed data from an unnamed government website without permission. OpenAI did not immediately respond to Fortune’s request for comment on which government website it was.
The website initially blocked the agent’s request, but the AI ultimately found a way to bypass the access controls. Multiple times along the way, the agent’s “chain of thought,” in which an agent writes down its reasoning steps, indicated that the model itself was questioning if its actions were “ethical,” but it ultimately proceeded.

On OpenAI’s side, another AI model that acted as an automated grader of the research task the other AI model was trying to fulfill did not consistently flag this behavior as problematic. It “marked some responses incorrect and others correct,” the report said. The way graders assess AI behavior can shape whether it occurs again. In a Sept. 11 essay on misalignment by Turing Award–winner Yoshua Bengio, he said the Hugging Face incident may have occurred because automated graders rewarded cheating and hacking in previous training runs.
“With the OpenAI agents, there is reason to believe successful cheating was actually rewarded: When the scoring program does not see the cheating, it pays out anyway, and such cheats become more likely next time,” Bengio said.

OpenAI says it has since improved its security as well as its alignment grading. “In response to this and to other incidents, we’ve strengthened our security controls, blocked models from accessing the live internet during training or evaluation, improved our alignment grading, and extended our misalignment monitoring to all reinforcement learning and evaluation traffic,” the company noted.
The most recent incident OpenAI has disclosed, which occurred on Oct. 6, involved one of the AI models the company uses as an automated grader. In that case, the grader tried to upload fraudulent reports on what it had found in an evaluation. This is an example of why relying on AI models to grade the training runs of other AI models can be problematic.

Making an unauthorized purchase with someone else’s cryptocurrency
In another disclosed case, a model in the GPT-5.6 Sol family—the predecessor to OpenAI’s current flagship model, GPT-6 Astra—accessed a cryptocurrency wallet the human testers had not provided it, and made an unauthorized payment to complete a task during testing. This occurred on June 26. OpenAI discovered it in September.

“The model questioned whether it had permission” to make the purchase, OpenAI said, again referring to what the model had recorded about its own reasoning in its chain of thought. It then reasoned with itself that since it found the information publicly, it could use it. In the model’s chain-of-thought logs, it figured that since the wallet it found was public, that “funds could be stolen anytime.”
It then concluded, “We can deploy!” It later asked itself again if the act was done “ethically,” and reasoned that the funds were “effectively abandoned.”

Getting internet access, changing live systems
The other incident OpenAI flagged as critical involved a model looking up public data, which theoretically is acceptable, but in the process it accessed the organization’s internal system, made changes to it, and was still able to “retain access … even after reverting the changes,” OpenAI said. It also downloaded 147,451 rows from nonpublic data tables. Perhaps most concerningly, the model did not disclose any of its actions to the evaluators.

In the final case OpenAI disclosed, an AI agent was able to get internet access from a research environment that should have been isolated—potentially similar to what happened during the Hugging Face incident, in which hundreds of AI agents were able to get internet access, although OpenAI did not directly compare these two incidents.
In the newly disclosed case, the agent knew it was not allowed to access the web, so it asked “external services” to perform actions it was blocked from doing. It did this even after it had found another way to answer the question, and also continued to develop its crafty work-around even after completing the task.
